SRC_2: Modern movies often look flat, plastic, and cheap despite having the biggest budgets in film history.
Some modern TV shows look more cinematic than movies currently shown in theaters.
The video argues that CGI, visual effects, AI, and filters are scapegoats and not the real reason movies look different now.
The first reason cited for the change is a shift to using much wider focal-length lenses than were traditionally used in cinema.
Wider lenses arrived alongside larger digital camera sensors, which also produced ultra-wide fields of view popular with YouTube content creators.
Wide lenses pull the camera physically closer to actors and the set, distorting perspective compared to traditional longer-lens, distance shooting.
Traditional film sets kept the camera at a distance, mimicking a natural human eye viewpoint, unlike modern intimate, vlog-like framing.
The second reason is faster lens apertures and shallower depth of field enabled by bigger digital sensors.
Traditional cinema was often shot on Super 35mm film at apertures like T5.6, T8, or T11 to keep sets, extras, and backgrounds in focus.
Achieving those smaller apertures on film required large amounts of light because film stock was relatively slow (low sensitivity).
Early digital camera sensors were small, keeping everything in focus and lacking the shallow depth of field seen in film.
The DSLR revolution introduced full-frame sensors capable of video, unlocking strong background blur (bokeh) as a popular aesthetic.
Modern filmmakers often shoot at very wide apertures like f/1.4, creating excessive blur that obscures backgrounds and extras, unlike traditional cinema.
The third reason is an obsession with maximizing dynamic range on digital sensors to avoid clipping highlights or shadows.
This dynamic-range obsession causes images to look flat and low-contrast because everything is kept within a narrow 10%-90% exposure range.
The human eye naturally experiences high contrast, such as being blinded stepping outside or seeing near-black indoors after being outside, which digital's uniform exposure doesn't replicate.
Alongside dynamic range chasing, filmmakers began over-using soft lighting tools like softboxes, domes, china balls, and book lights.
Old-school cinema used harsh, hard lighting from powerful lights to properly expose film and created shape, texture, and contrast.
Older camera lenses were optically imperfect and soft at fast apertures, discouraging filmmakers from shooting wide open even if possible.
A fourth reason is that improved sensor technology now allows very clean high ISO performance, reducing the perceived need for intentional lighting.
This has led to filmmakers relying on high ISO in dim environments instead of lighting scenes, producing flat, muddy, lifeless images.
Traditional night scenes in film, such as in Lord of the Rings, were deliberately lit bright and blue, appearing more cinematic than modern unlit, high-ISO night shots that resemble night vision.
A fifth reason is the modern trend of extremely long single-take shots (e.g., 'oner' shots), enabled by cheap and abundant digital recording.
Film reels had physical runtime limits, forcing filmmakers to work in precise, intentional shot-by-shot sequences with planned coverage via storyboarding.
Digital recording removes cost constraints, allowing filmmakers to roll for hours, which can lead long takes to dictate storytelling structure rather than serve it.
Long takes often require lights to be moved further away and cameras to be integrated into a full 360-degree environment, exaggerating the loss of the traditional 'distant' cinematic feel.
A sixth reason is constant, fluid camera movement enabled by small, lightweight cameras and gimbals or drones, which can make shots feel like video games rather than cinema.
Old-school cameras were large, heavy, and noisy, requiring fixed tripod setups and deliberate shot-by-shot filming, contrasting with today's mobile, handheld freedom.
The presenter states none of these new techniques are inherently bad, but their widespread, unbalanced use has eroded traditional cinematic feel.
Attempts to disguise modern digital aesthetics with film grain, black bars, or teal-and-orange color grading do not fix the underlying stylistic issues.
The presenter's children describe old movies as looking 'glitchy,' possibly referring to grain, harsh lighting, or old-fashioned acting styles.
The presenter argues perception of cinematic quality is generational, with younger viewers seeing old films as outdated rather than more cinematic.

The presenter suggests modern technology can still achieve a cinematic look by using deeper depth of field (stopping down aperture), pushing color grading for more contrast, and mixing in hard lighting alongside soft light.
The presenter recommends allowing actors to sweat or appear textured and imperfect, contrasting with the current trend of overly soft, polished imagery where nothing appears dirty or rough.

The overarching argument is that digital filmmaking initially tried to emulate film but overcorrected, pushing techniques like bokeh, dynamic range, and soft lighting past the point of natural cinematic balance.

The presenter concludes that fixing the cinematic look requires dialing back these overcompensations and refocusing on fundamentals like writing, storytelling, acting, editing, set dressing, wardrobe, hair, and makeup.
SRC_3: Video essayist Tom van der Linden created a YouTube documentary titled 'Why movies just don't feel real anymore'.
Tom van der Linden is the creator of the Like Stories of Old series on YouTube.
Van der Linden compares Jurassic World Rebirth, the seventh film in the Jurassic Park franchise, to the original 1993 Jurassic Park to explain why modern films feel less immersive.
Van der Linden gives five reasons why films no longer feel as 'real' as they used to: perceptual realism, the cinematic look, indexicality, haptic visuality, and cinematic qualia.
Perceptual realism argues that older films used more deep focus, keeping background objects in focus, which helps audiences feel immersed.
Deep focus allows viewers' eyes to scan the frame for spatial information similarly to how they perceive real-world environments.
Modern films often use shallow focus, showing a sharp foreground against a blurry background, which differs from natural human perception.

American philosopher Noël Carroll argued that deep focus, long-shot compositions invite audiences to scan the frame for meaning similarly to ordinary perceptual experience, making them feel more realistic.
In the original Jurassic Park, dinosaurs appear in a real-world environment, while in Jurassic World Rebirth they appear in an overly cinematic, digitally exaggerated version of Earth.
Digital manipulation lets filmmakers alter shots after filming, including changing backgrounds, altering performances, and creating camera movements that didn't happen on set.

Van der Linden argues that the shift from committing to an image on set to fixing it in post-production contributes to a feeling of fakeness in modern films, even when real locations or practical effects are used.
Indexicality refers to the idea that traditional celluloid film images are authentic because light physically struck the film to create the image.
Digital photography lacks indexicality because it uses sensors that convert light into an image rather than physically imprinting it.
Film has a natural motion blur created by a physical camera shutter, making action appear to move more smoothly than digital footage.
Film has a grainy visual texture, while digital images can show pixelated noise instead.
Digitally shot films tend to look sharper, while film-shot images tend to look warmer.
Philosopher and writer Laura Marks introduced the concept of 'haptic visuality,' the idea that films are experienced with the whole body, not just eyes and ears.
Haptic perception, according to psychologists, combines different ways humans perceive touch.
Older films with deeper focus and grainy texture provide a richer haptic sensory environment than modern films.
Cinematic qualia is a Latin-derived term meaning 'what it's like,' referring to the sensory authenticity of an experience in film.
Van der Linden argues that today's films often lack cinematic qualia compared to older films.
Van der Linden compares gritty, sweaty shots in Sorcerer (1977), starring Roy Scheider, to a similar humid tropical scene in Jurassic World Rebirth to illustrate differences in qualia.
In Sorcerer, actors appear to struggle realistically in their environment, while in Rebirth, flat lighting and vanity makeup make actors look comfortable rather than authentic.
Van der Linden concludes that no single factor explains why films feel less real; it's a combination of medium and execution changes over decades.
Van der Linden states that deep immersion arises from a continuous accumulation of shots and scenes rather than from any single image.
Van der Linden argues that immersion depends on combined sensory and technical elements including makeup, wardrobe, set dressing, sound design, and music.
Van der Linden states the goal of filmmaking is to transport, move, and touch audiences so they feel they experienced something real and meaningful.
Most modern films are shot digitally rather than on physical celluloid film, unlike the majority of films from 25 years ago.
Modern moviegoers are more likely to watch films at home than in theaters compared to previous decades.

In the late 1990s, CGI technology was less advanced, so filmmakers could only use it sparingly.
Steven Spielberg balanced practical effects and CGI in the first Jurassic Park movie and expanded on that balance in The Lost World.
In The Lost World, visceral moments like a T-Rex tongue were achieved using practical effects rather than CGI.

Modern movies often rely heavily on computers, green screens, or virtual production volumes for effects.

Spreading VFX artists thin across many CGI shots can lead to a decline in overall visual quality.

The author argues The Lost World: Jurassic Park's CGI looks good specifically because the film does not use CGI extensively.

SRC_6: Jurassic Park was released in 1993 and received a 20th anniversary theatrical re-release.
In the two decades since 1993, CGI visual effects became commonplace and utilitarian, appearing even in romantic comedies and family dramas.
DragonHeart, released a couple of years after Jurassic Park, now looks more like a cartoon than a photorealistic film.
Spider-Man's effects looked flimsy and thin within less than a decade of release.
The later Harry Potter movies' effects already looked dated while still in theaters.
The only bad CGI shot in Jurassic Park is the first brachiosaur shot, and the flaw is due to lighting rather than the model or animation.
Jurassic Park's filmmakers relied primarily on animatronics and used CGI only for creatures that could not be created practically on set.
Because CGI creatures are shown as real the first time audiences see them, viewers are trained to believe in them rather than hunt for fake effects.
Using less CGI overall meant more attention could be lavished on each individual CGI frame in Jurassic Park.
The VFX artists hid effects flaws by placing key CGI sequences in low light, such as the T-Rex chasing the jeep in rain and the T-Rex fighting raptors in dusky park headquarters.
The brachiosaurs-at-sunset scene is another example of CGI hidden by low light.
The gallimimus stampede, the one major effects sequence in full daylight, hides flaws using high speed and motion blur instead of darkness.
Modern movies with CGI everywhere must present effects in plain view without such cheats, unlike Jurassic Park.
In 2013, audiences are so accustomed to CGI that even bad CGI effects fade into the background and don't hurt a film commercially.
Weak effects in The Avengers or The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey do not cost those franchises money because audiences have become inured to CGI limitations.
In 1993, there was no similar acceptance of flawed effects, so Jurassic Park's filmmakers had to invest maximum time, energy, and money to get the dinosaur effects exactly right.
Avatar is described as a movie whose sole point was presenting the most immersive CGI world ever created rather than telling a compelling story or introducing exciting characters.
The argument claims Avatar risks becoming a historical footnote once a more immersive CGI world is created.
Jurassic Park is described as fundamentally a movie about dinosaurs running amok and killing people, using CGI only to make that premise tangible.
The effects in Jurassic Park hold up because they are not meant to draw attention to themselves, so viewers are too busy following the action to notice compositing issues.

Steven Spielberg used a similar sleight-of-hand approach 18 years earlier in Jaws, where the mechanical shark looks worse than any Jurassic Park effect but doesn't matter because audiences are already invested in the story.
The first brachiosaur scene is the only moment in Jurassic Park where CGI is meant to be gawked at, and it is the weakest effects work in the film.
Gollum and Life of Pi's Richard Parker are cited as two of the best CGI creations of the 21st century because they serve the story rather than being meant to impress on their own.
A reader comment states that Laura Dern's gaping-mouth reaction shot to the first dinosaur is also considered a weak special effect moment.
A reader comment explains that the animatronics used on set were reportedly digitized/programmed into computers and manipulated like the physical puppets, a process similar to motion capture.

A reader comment argues that theme park dark-ride animatronics (like Disney's Dinosaur ride in Animal Kingdom) work well because darkness conceals the mechanism, similar to Jurassic Park's low-light CGI approach.

A reader comment compares this darkness effect to haunted house illusions like claustrophobia rooms and vortex tunnels, arguing that concealing the mechanism of an effect helps audiences accept it as real.
A reader comment claims all the CGI was retouched for the Jurassic Park 3D re-release because the original animal textures didn't hold up under the rotoscoping process.
A reader comment argues the effects still look good because dinosaurs are based on real animals rather than fantastical creatures like dragons, giving them verisimilitude.

A reader comment argues that because no one has seen a real dinosaur, audiences can't easily judge CGI dinosaur inaccuracies, whereas CGI elephants would be more easily judged as low quality since real elephants are commonly seen.
One reader comment states the sound work in Jurassic Park might be even better than the visual effects.
One reader comment attributes the film's visual quality simply to the fact that the filmmakers 'spared no expense.'
